title: Product pages that explain the thing, then step aside
metaTitle: Ecommerce product page design, object first
excerpt: Lead a product page with the object, the price, and the one reason it exists. Materials, shipping, and the longer story come after a decision is possible.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first screen of a product page?
faqs.answer: Show the object, the price, and one sentence on why it exists, then the action to buy. Nielsen Norman Group reported in 2011 that people often leave a page in 10 to 20 seconds and read only about a quarter of the text. The longer story can sit below, for the person who stays.

faqs.question: Where should materials and shipping go?
faqs.answer: After the first screen can stand alone. Order the rest by the questions a skeptical buyer asks: materials and dimensions, shipping and returns, a photograph that shows scale, then the longer note. If a fact changes whether they should buy, keep it out of a collapsed panel.

faqs.question: How should variants appear?

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Ecommerce product page design should make a decision possible, then get out of the way. Lead with the object, the price, and the one reason this thing exists. Shipping, materials, sizing, and the longer story come after that, for the person who is still looking. A page that opens with a manifesto makes the shopper hunt for the thing they clicked.

The page has one job. Help someone understand this object well enough to buy it, save it, or leave without feeling misled.

## The first screen is the decision

Put the photograph of the object first. Not a lifestyle crop so tight that the object is a texture. The shopper should be able to say what they are looking at. Next to it, or directly under it on a phone, put the name, the price, and one sentence on why it exists. The sentence is the job of the object, in the brand's voice. A waxed cotton jacket that sheds rain on a commute. A mug that fits under a coffee machine. Specific beats atmospheric.

Then the action. Add to bag, or whatever the brand calls that verb, as long as it is the same verb everywhere. If a variant changes the object, show that choice here too, and show it as the thing itself where you can: a color, a size, a length. Do not hide the price behind the choice. If the price changes with the variant, the price updates when the choice does.

Jakob Nielsen, writing for Nielsen Norman Group in 2011, reported that people often leave a web page in 10 to 20 seconds, and that a page has to communicate its value within about 10 seconds if it wants longer attention. He also noted that people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on the pages they actually visit. A product page that spends the first screen on a brand essay spends the only seconds it is likely to get. The essay can live further down for the person who stays. The object, the price, and the reason have to be present before that patience is required. The research is [How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/).

## What comes after the decision is possible

Once the first screen can stand alone, the rest of the page is support. Order it by the questions a skeptical buyer asks, not by the departments that produced the answers.

- What is it made of, and what is it not. Materials, dimensions, and the care they imply.
- How it will arrive. Shipping window, returns, and the cost if it is not already in the price.
- How it looks in use, in a second photograph that shows scale. A hand, a room, a body, whichever tells the truth of the size.
- The longer note. Origin, process, or a detail a fan will enjoy. This is where voice can stretch, because the decision no longer depends on it.

Keep each block short. A wall of accordions that are all collapsed is a hiding place. Open the one fact people always need, such as sizing or allergens, and let the rest be a scroll. If a fact changes whether the person should buy, it does not belong in a footnote.

The photograph and the words have to agree. If the picture shows a set and the price is for one piece, say that in the first screen, not after the description. Disagreement on the first screen is how a page creates a return and a grudge.

## Variants, stock, and the quiet states

Show the choice that changes the object. Hide the matrix. A list of every combination, with codes, is an inventory screen. The shopper is picking a color and a size, or a single option. When a combination is unavailable, say so on that choice and offer the nearest one that can ship. Do not dump them on an error, and do not let them add a dead variant to the bag.

Out of stock is a state of this page, not a different website. Keep the object visible, keep the price if you are willing to, and say when it returns if you know. A page that vanishes teaches people not to bother coming back.

Images need text alternatives that describe the object, including the variant if the image is variant-specific. The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treat those alternatives as part of making content perceivable, and the same standard asks that the controls be operable. A color choice that is only a colored circle, with no name, fails a shopper who cannot see the circle and a shopper whose screen renders the color poorly. The name is the interface. The swatch is support.

## A page that steps aside

Stepping aside means the page does not keep pitching after the facts are available. Related products, if you show them, come after the support, and they are a few honest pairings. A row of twenty lookalikes above the price is the page refusing to let the object speak.

Reviews, if you have real ones, sit with the support. An average with no way to read the substance is decoration. Do not invent praise, and do not write a review in the brand's voice and attribute it to a customer. If you have no reviews yet, omit the module. An empty stars widget looks like a broken claim.

The button stays available as the person scrolls, on a phone especially, once they have seen the price. Repeating the price near the button is a kindness. Repeating three promotional banners is the page getting back in the way.

Hanabi's public shop work includes the ecommerce restructure, migration, and redesign of Down the Cove, a move that left WooCommerce. The standard on a product page is the same one the studio states for the rest of the work: clarity over complexity. The object leads. The longer story does not have to be deleted. It has to wait its turn.

## The grid that feeds the page

A product page cannot rescue a grid of mismatched crops. People arrive with an expectation set by the thumbnail. If the thumbnail was a tight texture and the page is a full object, they feel misled before they read the sentence. The companion to this page is the wall they came from: [photography, crop, and the product grid](/blog/photography-and-the-product-grid).

Consistent photographs make the first screen easier, because the object is already what they thought they clicked.

The shops where this kind of page has to hold up are in [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Look at whether you can see the object, the price, and the reason without a hunt.
